result.markdown: --- format: html practical: Practical_3_Probability doc-id: "0301" author: "Katy Brown" --- # Part 1: Loops {#sec-p2_loops} ::: {.callout-note .partmenu #parts-0301} ## Sections - @sec-loops - @sec-storing_results - @sec-repeat_samples - @sec-summary_0301 ::: ::: {.callout-tip .objectives #objectives-0301} #### Learning objectives By the end of this part of the practical you will be able to: - Explain the purpose of a `for` loop in programming. - Use a `for` loop to repeat a task. - Store results generated using a loop. - Apply loops to process multiple datasets. ::: In this practical, you will need two Quarto documents: * `prac3_exercises.qmd` for basic exercises * `squirrels.qmd` for a squirrel based simulation exercise * `drosophila.qmd` for investigating mutation counts in Drosophila * `distributions.qmd` for quick investigations of different probability distributions ## For Loops {#sec-loops} A loop is a way of repeating a task multiple times in a computer program. There are two main types of loop, a **for loop**, which runs once for every item in a vector (or other sequence), or a **while loop** which runs until a certain condition is met. In this part of the practical we will focus on **for loops**, which perform a task a fixed number of times. We usually loop over a vector, meaning we perform the task once for each item in the vector. To repeat a task `n` times, we can use `seq_len(n)`. This creates a sequence from `1` to `n`. The loop then runs `n` times, once for each number in this sequence. If we run our loop as `for (i in seq_len(n))`, each time we pass through the loop, the value of `i` increases by one. We refer to each pass through the loop as an **iteration** - we **iterate** over a loop. In a loop, like in a function, we use curly brackets `{}` to show which code is part of the loop - so everything inside the brackets will be repeated every time we iterate through the loop. For example: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} for (i in seq_len(10)) { print(i) } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 [1] 2 [1] 3 [1] 4 [1] 5 [1] 6 [1] 7 [1] 8 [1] 9 [1] 10 ``` ::: ::: We can add steps to our loop to run on each iteration. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} for (i in seq_len(10)) { # add 2 to i j <- i + 2 # take the square root of j sj <- sqrt(j) # round sj to the nearest whole number rsj <- round(sj) # print rsj print(rsj) } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2 [1] 2 [1] 2 [1] 2 [1] 3 [1] 3 [1] 3 [1] 3 [1] 3 [1] 3 ``` ::: ::: We also don't have to actually use our variable `i` inside the loop, we can just use it to set the number of iterations. ::: {.callout-exercise #ex-loops_1} In your `prac3_exercises.qmd` quarto document, generate two for loops: 1. A `for` loop which calculates and prints the **cube** of each number from 1 to 20. ::: {.callout-note #note-powers} The operator `^` is used for powers in R, so e.g. 2^2 is 2 squared, 4^12 is 4 to the power of 12. ::: 2. This code snippet generates a random 5 letter character string. `paste(sample(letters, 5, replace = TRUE), collapse="")` Using a `for` loop, generate 5 such strings. ::: {.callout-answer collapse="true" #ex-loops_1_ans} A `for` loop which calculates and prints the **cube** of each number from 1 to 20. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} for (i in seq_len(20)) { print(i^3) } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 [1] 8 [1] 27 [1] 64 [1] 125 [1] 216 [1] 343 [1] 512 [1] 729 [1] 1000 [1] 1331 [1] 1728 [1] 2197 [1] 2744 [1] 3375 [1] 4096 [1] 4913 [1] 5832 [1] 6859 [1] 8000 ``` ::: ::: This code snippet generates a random 5 letter character string. `paste(sample(letters, 5, replace = TRUE), collapse="")` Using a `for` loop, generate 5 such strings. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} for (i in seq_len(5)) { print(paste(sample(letters, 5, replace = TRUE), collapse = "")) } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "zsnok" [1] "gaxnb" [1] "zssse" [1] "kdsun" [1] "jvdrn" ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: You can also use a for loop to do something to each item in a vector. For example, in the below, we loop through the animals in our vector `species`. Inside the loop, the value of the variable `spp` changes on each iteration. The cowsay package uses the `say()` function and the argument by = [animal_name]{.orange-text} (where [animal_name]{.orange-text} is the name of an animal) to print ascii art of animals (and their associates) saying things. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(cowsay) species <- c("frog", "stegosaurus", "squirrel", "ghost") for (spp in species) { say(paste("I am your friend, a", spp), by = spp) } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` __________________________ < I am your friend, a frog > -------------------------- \ \ (.)_(.) _ ( _ ) _ / \/`-----'\/ \ __\ ( ( ) ) /__ ) /\ \._./ /\ ( )_/ /|\ /|\ \_( [nosig] _________________________________ < I am your friend, a stegosaurus > --------------------------------- \ \ . . / `. .' \ .---. < > < > .---. | \ \ - ~ ~ - / / | ~-..-~ ~-..-~ \~~~\.' `./~~~/ .-~~^-. \__/ \__/ .' For example, let's write a short story about bird migration, based on what we learned in practical 2. The `cat()` function works like `print()`, but doesn't print each output on a new line. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cat("A bird leaves west Africa.\n") for (i in seq_len(25)) { cat("flap ") } cat("The bird arrives in Europe\n") cat("6 months later...\n") cat("A bird leaves Europe\n") for (i in seq_len(100)) { cat("flap ") } cat("\nThe bird arrives in west Africa.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` A bird leaves west Africa. flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap The bird arrives in Europe 6 months later... A bird leaves Europe flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap flap The bird arrives in west Africa. ``` ::: ::: Everything inside the brackets is repeated, everything outside of the brackets is not. ## Storing results from loops {#sec-storing_results} We sometimes want to store the results of running our loop in a vector or data frame. For example, here we store all of the cubed numbers from our example above in a vector called `cubed_nums`. Before we start the loop, we create an empty vector using `c()`. Then, each time we pass through the loop, we use `c()` again to append the new result to the end of the vector. Once the loop has finished, `cubed_nums` contains the results from every iteration. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cubed_nums <- c() for (i in seq_len(20)) { res <- i^3 cubed_nums <- c(cubed_nums, res) } print(cubed_nums) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 8 27 64 125 216 343 512 729 1000 1331 1728 2197 2744 3375 [16] 4096 4913 5832 6859 8000 ``` ::: ::: ## Review {#sec-summary_0301} [↑ top](#) ::: {.callout-note #note-summary_0301} ### Programming summary * A `for` loop repeats a task a fixed number of times. * Each cycle through a loop is called an **iteration**. * You usually use a vector to determine the iterations of the loop. * You can store the results of your loop by adding to a vector in each iteration. ::: For this part of the practical, the main files you have edited are: * `prac3_exercises.qmd` These are the files you should select when making your Git commit. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Commit your changes Remember to save your progress regularly by committing your changes with Git. 1. Save your changes to the files above in RStudio with the `Save` button. 2. Render any Quarto documents with the `Render` button. 3. Open the `Git` tab in RStudio. 4. Tick the files listed above, don't worry about any others. 5. Click `Commit` and write a short message in the `Commit message` describing your changes, something like e.g. "Practical 1 part 1" is sufficient, then click `Commit`. Close the `Commit` popup. :::
